## TrailFold — weekly client update

### 30-day performance snapshot
These are **30-day comparisons**, not a weekly trend or a controlled experiment.

- Sessions increased from 20,000 to 25,000 (**+25%**), while orders fell from 600 to 500 (**−16.7%**).
- Net product revenue fell from $54,000 to $45,000 (**−16.7%**). Average revenue per order remained approximately **$90**.
- Session-based conversion fell from **3.0% to 2.0%** (**−33.3%**).
- The largest visible weakness is mobile: mobile conversion fell from **2.67% to 1.50%**, while desktop remained **4.0%** in both periods.
- Add-to-cart sessions were flat at 10% of sessions. Checkout starts fell from 60% to 50% of add-to-cart sessions; orders per checkout start remained 50%. These are session-based counts, so they identify where to investigate rather than proving a user-level cause.

### What the Meta/Shopify discrepancy means
Meta reported $70,400 of purchase value on $22,000 spend, or **3.2x reported ROAS**, versus $54,000 on $18,000 spend, or **3.0x** previously. However, Shopify records only $45,000 of current-period net product revenue. Meta therefore reports **$25,400 more purchase value than Shopify revenue** for the current 30 days. The prior periods happened to match at $54,000, but that does not validate the current attribution.

The systems use different attribution windows and definitions: Meta uses 7-day click/1-day view, Klaviyo uses 5-day click/5-day open, and Meta value has not been reconciled to Shopify orders. The gap can include attribution overlap, view-through credit, returning-customer orders, timing, or configuration differences. We should not scale spend based on Meta ROAS until it reconciles to Shopify/P&L data. No revenue uplift is being claimed.

## Three priorities
1. **Reconcile channel reporting to Shopify and contribution economics.** Build one current-period view using Shopify net revenue, ad spend, product/delivery costs, and new-versus-returning orders. Treat Meta and Klaviyo attributed revenue as directional until reconciled.
2. **Investigate the mobile conversion and checkout drop.** Update the PDP’s opening message to “An 18L daypack for workdays and short trips,” move the 13-inch laptop-sleeve specification and 4–7 business-day delivery estimate above reviews, and state “water-resistant, not waterproof.” Do not claim 15-inch laptop compatibility until confirmed.
3. **Protect Daypack availability while improving qualified demand.** At the current 8 units/day velocity, 210 units provide about 26 days of coverage; replenishment arrives in 35 days. Do not increase Daypack acquisition spend now. The go decision is: proceed only when the owner confirms a stock/fulfilment plan covering the estimated gap and measurement is reconciled; otherwise hold incremental spend and use existing inventory for controlled creative/PDP learning only.

## Decisions needed from the owner
- Approve the proposed PDP headline, specification placement, and plain-language water-resistance clarification; approve or provide verified 15-inch laptop dimensions.
- Approve the inventory-aware no-scale rule for Daypack spend and confirm whether any units are reserved for wholesale, replacements, or other commitments.
- Approve access to Shopify order exports and ad/email spend data for a reconciled contribution view. No discount is proposed.

## Internal task board
| Task | Owner | Dependency | Acceptance check | Hours |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Reconcile Shopify, Meta, and Klaviyo period totals; separate new/returning where available | Owner | Shopify export and spend definitions | One table showing net revenue, orders, spend, attributed revenue, and unexplained variance | 2 |
| Calculate Daypack coverage and document spend go/no-go status | Owner | Confirmed inventory commitments and reservations | Coverage uses 8/day, 35-day arrival, and a clearly stated gap/risk; status is “hold incremental spend” unless approved plan exists | 1 |
| Approve PDP changes and verify laptop-fit wording | Owner | Product specification confirmation | Written approval or corrections supplied to designer/developer | 1 |
| Produce mobile-first PDP hero/specification layout | Designer | Owner-approved copy | Design contains approved headline, 18L, 13-inch sleeve, water-resistant—not waterproof, and delivery estimate above reviews | 4 |
| Produce laptop-fit comparison creative without unsupported claims | Designer | Verified dimensions or explicit 13-inch-only wording | Two variants delivered with no 15-inch claim and clear product context | 2 |
| Prepare controlled mobile PDP/checkout implementation | Developer | Approved design and copy | Changes staged, mobile QA completed, and no checkout or shipping-policy regression found | 3 |
| Add measurement notes/events for PDP view, add-to-cart, and checkout-start review | Developer | Access to Shopify theme/analytics setup | Event definitions documented; no claim of incrementality | 1 |

[2b34d63c3b0e9a1a1a46a7c2] Reconcile Platform Data Against the P&L
Applies when: You are auditing your measurement setup or preparing a board/CFO review of marketing spend efficiency.
- Start from the P&L and work backwards: profit contribution = revenue − cost of delivery − marketing. New-customer profit contribution = new-customer revenue − its delivery cost − its marketing cost.
- Ask whether the platform-reported numbers can defend themselves internally: which metric would you stand behind if the CFO challenged whether a channel actually drove revenue?
- For churn-heavy or high-return categories (fashion, supplements), use net revenue rather than gross revenue — returns will otherwise make today's ROAS look good and tomorrow's P&L worse.
- Build a single reconciled view: CFO headline = profit contribution; then AMER, new-customer revenue/orders; then CAC; then profit contribution detail. High accuracy comes from basing metrics on actual financials rather than modeled attribution.
- Where platform and P&L disagree, investigate before scaling: often platform ROAS is inflated by view-through, existing-customer bleed-over or a halo event. Don't add another attribution tool to resolve the gap — subtract noise and reconcile to financials.
Condition: Source says finance-grade reconciliation loses reliability as the business introduces more channels and complexity; above roughly high-eight-figure scale, lift studies may be required to attribute revenue to specific channels.

[4f1e89e8a7983a564e1122a0] Diagnose Growth Bottlenecks Through a Data-Integrity First Lens
Applies when: You feel like the store is 'on a treadmill' — dashboards show improving ROAS but profit and revenue are flat, and you need to decide where to focus resources (merchandise, creative, media, retention) next quarter.
- Frame the business as three stacked pillars: data integrity/measurement at the base, creative velocity/diversity in the middle, technical account structure on top. The source argues the upper layers are meaningless if the base is wrong, because you'll be optimizing creative and budgets against false signals.
- Recognize that a business grows by repeatedly solving one bottleneck at a time — when one is solved, another appears. So the recurring task is not 'do everything' but 'find the current constraint fast' and resource it.
- Use accurate, commercially-aligned data to locate the bottleneck: platform-reported ROAS, CPA and multi-touch numbers are the least reliable tier; finance-grade metrics (profit contribution, MER/AMER) are more reliable; controlled lift studies are the most causal but slowest to read.
- Example of the failure mode: an ad reads 4x ROAS, so you brief more ads like it and increase spend; ROAS dips to 3x but you reinforce the same decision. If the original 4x was inflated, every downstream decision (creative briefs, budget shifts, staffing) is wrong while profit stays flat.
- Practical output: before allocating next quarter's resource, verify which pillar is actually failing — if you cannot reconcile marketing claims to the P&L, data integrity is the bottleneck regardless of what the channel dashboards say.
Condition: The claim that data integrity is the bottleneck in ~30% of audited businesses is the presenter's own audit experience, not a universal benchmark.
Condition: The 2026 framing (iOS deprecation, modeled conversions) is time-specific; verify current platform behavior before relying on details.

[8d570963a07c01bd206aac7f] Five core finance practices to run an ecommerce brand
Applies when: Setting your store's monthly financial operating rhythm or auditing which finance disciplines your team is missing before scaling spend.
- 1) Know your gross margin and calculate it correctly: identify variable costs, and distinguish product margin from gross margin and how each flows into contribution margin. Use these definitions consistently across the team.
- 2) Define your metrics and build live dashboards—not daily ROAS reports. Track acquisition MER, profit contribution, and ideally LTGP to CAC. The source argues weekly ROAS reporting is unproductive for core decision-making.
- 3) Separate new vs returning customer metrics: track new-customer economics, acquisition MER, new-customer profit contribution, new-customer revenue and new-customer cohort size separately, because the underlying levers differ (and feed forecasting).
- Coordinate inventory and advertising: additional borrowing raises interest expense and reduces cash/net profit. Interest alone does not change MER (revenue/ad spend); model sales and spend separately.
- 5) Use the P&L to identify the constraint in the business: structure it out, set KPIs at each level, and when you fall below target look above that level in the P&L to find what changed and which lever to pull.
- Attribute the daily-vs-weekly ROAS stance to the source as an opinion, not a universal rule.
Condition: The daily-vs-weekly ROAS preference is the presenter's opinion, not an established benchmark.
Condition: The five-point list is a summary framework; it does not define numeric thresholds for any metric.

[94c5d797f80b138ba47d3111] Build a Weekly Forecasting Rhythm Even as a Solo Operator
Applies when: You need a repeatable operating cadence to keep sourced products in stock and profitable, whether you are solo or have a small team.
- Create a simple system that forces a performance and stock-level review every single week.
- Include daily sales velocity, total lead time and safety stock in the same sheet you use for the reorder point calculation.
- Communicate stock and forecast positions to suppliers proactively, before problems appear.
- If possible, designate one person focused purely on operations and planning rather than splitting the role.
- Start planning the next shipment when the current one lands, since production plus transit can consume 50-70 days in total.
- Treat the failure mode as a planning failure, not bad luck: the source describes a demand spike to $200,000/day sales followed by a sellout, months-long lead times and nearly two months unable to fulfill orders.
- The source believes a dedicated operations/planning focus could have made that business 30-40% bigger — its own retrospective estimate, not a universal figure.
Condition: The 30-40% upside figure is the source's retrospective opinion about its own business, not a benchmark for yours.
Condition: The source states you do not need a full team to start — discipline and a weekly cadence suffice initially.

[bcee1e69de7698ae45475b5d] The Daily 3: Cut to Three Needle-Movers
Applies when: Weekly planning for a lean ecommerce team or solo operator overwhelmed by merchandising, marketing, and ops tasks.
- Each morning (or the night before), list everything you could do across your store — product pages, ads, inventory, email, support.
- Force-rank and select only 3 tasks that most move the needle (e.g. fix the top PDP, launch the restock email, resolve a checkout drop-off).
- Work top to bottom through those 3 before touching anything else.
- Say no to the other 97% deliberately; defer, delegate, or delete them.
- Review the pattern over weeks so recurring 'yes' items reflect your real priorities, not noise.
Condition: Source is the presenter's personal operating rule, not a proven system for all teams.
Condition: Some urgent ops issues (stockouts, payment failures) may need same-day handling outside the 3.

[2df157249026bbe0fbaa206c] Balance Attribution and Profitability Metrics in Your Owned Media KPIs
Applies when: Setting the reporting dashboard for your email/SMS retention program, or deciding what changes your retention team should make.
- Treat platform attribution metrics (account/campaign/flow attributed revenue, revenue per recipient, 30-50% revenue share from email) as an indicator only. They show whether you're reaching enough people, whether flows exist and whether cadence is sensible.
- Take attribution with a grain of salt: outside studies cited by the source suggest roughly 70-80% of campaign revenue may be incremental for some accounts, but it varies heavily by brand. Bigger brands can run incrementality tests.
- Balance with profitability metrics: LTGP adjusted for 90 and 365 days, mapped at 30/60/90/180/365 day cohorts, plus revenue from the top 20% of customers.
- Avoid both extremes: chasing attribution alone means you optimise for looking good in dashboards; ignoring incremental repeat-revenue work in favour of pure long-term LTV means you never improve today's numbers.
- Use attribution as the north star and profitability metrics as the constraint-finding tool that sets your retention targets.
Condition: The 30-50% revenue share figure is described as a soft indicator, not hard science.
Condition: Attribution and metric availability may change — verify current Klaviyo interface before building dashboards.
